title: Design for high availability
learningObjective: Recommend high availability for compute, relational data and semi-structured and unstructured data, and calculate composite SLAs.
foundation: High availability means the app keeps running when a part fails. Availability zones protect against a datacenter failure; a second region protects against a regional one.
Every service has an SLA. When an app needs several services at once, their SLAs multiply, so the whole is less available than each part. Redundant copies raise availability again.
engineer: Compute: spread VMs or VM Scale Sets (Flexible orchestration) across availability zones behind a zone-redundant Standard Load Balancer or Application Gateway v2; use zone-redundant App Service plans, Container Apps environments, AKS node pools across zones and Functions on zone-redundant plans. Availability sets only for regions without zones. Multi-region: active-passive (warm or cold standby) or active-active behind Front Door or Traffic Manager, with health probes and automated failover.

Relational data: Azure SQL Database and Managed Instance include built-in HA; enable zone redundancy for zone failures; use active geo-replication or failover groups for regional resilience and readable secondaries. SQL Server on VMs: Always On availability groups across zones or regions. PostgreSQL and MySQL flexible server: zone-redundant HA with a standby replica.

Semi-structured and unstructured data: Cosmos DB with availability zones and multiple regions (service-managed failover; multi-region writes for the highest availability, with conflict resolution); storage redundancy ZRS, GZRS or RA-GZRS; RA- endpoints let apps read during a regional outage.

Composite SLA: services needed in series multiply (99.95% × 99.99% ≈ 99.94%). N independent copies in parallel: 1 − (1 − SLA)^N. Add the global router's SLA in series. Use the Well-Architected Framework reliability pillar to set targets, find single points of failure and design health modelling.

animation.caption: Pick zone, set or multi-region designs, data HA options, and calculate composite SLAs.

example.title: 99.99% for an online shop
body: Single region: App Service (zone-redundant), SQL Database (zone-redundant) and a cache give about 99.84% composite — below target. The architect deploys the stack in two regions, active-active behind Front Door.

Two regions raise the stack to about 99.9997% before the router; multiplied by Front Door's SLA the design clears 99.99%. Product data uses Cosmos DB with multi-region writes; images use RA-GZRS storage.

prerequisites: An Azure subscription; most design reviews need only Reader access
permissions: Reader to review existing resources; Contributor or Owner to build the design
limits: Check service limits and regional availability for each component
portal: App Service plan > Zone redundancy; VM Scale Set > Availability zones.
SQL database > Compute + storage > Zone redundancy; Failover groups.
Cosmos DB > Replicate data globally; Multi-region writes.
configuration.cli:
az appservice plan create -g rg-web -n asp-shop --sku P1v3 --zone-redundant --number-of-workers 2
az sql db update -g rg-data -s sql-weu -n db-shop --zone-redundant true
az cosmosdb update -g rg-data -n cosmos-shop --enable-multiple-write-locations true

troubleshooting.symptom: Downtime during a zone outage even though VMs were in a scale set.
troubleshooting.cause: Scale set not spread across zones.
troubleshooting.fix: Deploy the scale set across zones 1, 2 and 3 with a zone-redundant load balancer.

troubleshooting.symptom: Composite availability is lower than every single service's SLA.
troubleshooting.fix: Remove dependencies, add redundancy or a second region.

comparisons.difference: Active-active serves from both regions (higher cost, near-zero failover); active-passive keeps a standby (lower cost, longer RTO).
Zones: one region, survives a datacenter outage; geo: another region, survives a regional outage.

misconceptions.reality: The app's availability is the product of everything it depends on.

misconceptions.myth: Availability sets protect against datacenter failure.
misconceptions.reality: They protect against rack failures inside one datacenter.

architectureDecisions: Second region only when RTO/SLA needs it.
Calculate composite SLA and remove single points of failure.

steps.label: Problem
steps.title: The target is 99.99%
body: The business wants less than 5 minutes of downtime a month. Where can things fail, and what does each part promise?

steps.label: Compute
steps.title: Zones, sets and regions
body: Spread instances across availability zones (separate datacenters) behind a zone-redundant load balancer. Availability sets only protect against rack failures, for regions without zones. A second region protects against regional failure.

steps.label: Relational
steps.title: SQL stays up
body: Turn on zone redundancy for zone failures. Add geo-replication or a failover group for regional failures and readable secondaries.

steps.label: Other data
steps.title: Cosmos DB and storage
body: Cosmos DB with zones and multiple regions; multi-region writes for the highest availability. Storage with ZRS, GZRS or RA-GZRS for reads during a regional outage.

steps.label: The maths
steps.title: Composite SLA
body: Things you need together multiply: 99.95% × 99.99% × 99.9% ≈ 99.84%. Two independent copies: 1 − (1 − 0.9984)² ≈ 99.9997%. Then multiply by the router's SLA.

steps.title: HA design
recap: Zones by default; sets only without zones; regions for regional failure
